en: Preface to the Continued Lamp Archives:

If one wishes to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, one should contemplate the causes and conditions of time and season. In the past, when the World-Honored One held up a flower, Kāśyapa broke into a smile;
when Bodhidharma faced the wall, Huìnéng cut off his arm to find peace of mind. Reaching down to the era of Caoxi and beyond, following [this lineage]...
The flowing benefit became ever more enduring and the surging waves ever more expansive. As the chanting grew higher, the spiritual capacity of the practitioners became ever more sublime.

The stream branched into five houses, each establishing its own lineage and courtyard. Some were like lightning rolling or the wind racing; some were solitary, perilous, and toweringly steep; some were as dense and subtle as a golden needle;

some were father and son meeting on the same pivot; and some were like the tips of arrows meeting in flight. Their causes, conditions, seasons, and occasions differ in a thousand ways and ten thousand variations, each being distinct. If...

If the beginning and end were not fully recorded, from where could later students draw upon for verification? This is the reason for the composition of the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp).
Since the *Chuan deng lu* appeared during the Jingde era, there have subsequently followed the *Guang deng lu*, the *Xu deng lu*, the *Lian deng lu*, and the *Pu deng lu*.

Furthermore, during the Shaoxing era, the Grand Master Jigong of Dachuang held the primary position; his followers were distributed and spread abroad, their brilliance soaring and their colors overflowing, such that his teachings flourished throughout the Song dynasty.
From the end of the Song, through the Yuan and Ming dynasties, down to the present day.
For over four hundred years in this sagely age, although the three schools of the Mui (Muzhou), Yang (Yangshan),

and Yunmen lineages have unfortunately lacked successors, passing one after another until they were no longer transmitted, the two branches of Linji and Caodong have continued unbroken, their lineages flourishing together in successive generations.
Yet, alas, there has been a profound silence, with no one appearing to carry on their work, causing these great masters of the Dharma to fade into oblivion.
There was no record of it; ruined steles and broken tablets lay buried amidst the wild weeds and decaying brush.

How much more than a single thread hanging over the Nine Cauldrons was the ancestral life-force of wisdom! Long ago, Nanjian felt this deep anxiety and devoted himself to collecting and gathering [the fragments].
Every time he went out to seek them, he did not hesitate to travel thousands of li. In the summer of the Renwu year of the Chongzhen era, he happened to be in Yunjian and met Shi...
The Adjutant and Layman of Lize obtained the collection he had compiled; though they had not consulted one another, their views coincided. Thereupon, he returned home with a sense of vast serenity.
He took up his brush and devoted himself to the task for several years until the compilation was finally completed as a book.

Just as he was planning to commission craftsmen to carve the woodblocks, he encountered a period of chaotic upheaval and, fearing for its safety, concealed it once more. He titled it *Xudeng Cuncao* (Drafts for the Continued Lamp), but before the project could be implemented, he met with misfortune.
My late master once said abruptly: "For more than ten years since my passing, I have lived in seclusion on the remote frontiers, where my strength does not follow my will.
I reflect deeply that the years are passing away; how much time remains for tomorrow? To plant one's feet and pat one's thighs—how can there be any further delay?

My disciple Dinglang Ping was able to share in the concerns of others and took up this burden with resolute resolve, wishing to be as close as a single hair to the eyebrows of the various patriarchs and ancestral masters.
I tie up my breath in a single exhalation. Alas! Such are the seasonal conditions and causal circumstances.
If future gentlemen should continue this work, perhaps expanding upon it from this point forward so that the lamp may not fall out of sight, then how could these teachings ever come to an end?
On the day before the Mid-Autumn Festival in the Bingwu year of the Kangxi era, the Dharma-heir monk Longqiu Xingyu of Nanjian in Wulin,
having bathed and purified himself,

respectfully offers this brief note in search of the recorded sayings and funerary inscriptions (taming) of Chan masters of the Great Ming, in order to fully continue the *Fozu Tongji* (Transmission of the Lamp).

I humbly reflect that since the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye was entrusted by the World-Honored One to Kāśyapa, and from the time Bodhidharma first crossed to the East to point directly to the human mind,
the lineage has been transmitted from lamp to lamp with its respective records serving as the eyes for humans and devas.

Yet, in our own sovereign nation, nearly three hundred years have passed since the transmission of the lamp was interrupted and severed, causing the patriarchs of this flourishing era to fall into obscurity.
He passed away without having heard [the Dharma]. Those who know him grieve for him. Master Daguan’s aspirations were not fulfilled;

as he was about to enter nirvana, he lamented that the transmission of the lamp had not yet been continued, saying, "This is a great failure for my life of wisdom. Reading the Collected Works of Zibo, I could not contain my feelings of indignation.
Coincidentally, because my family possesses a collection of books, I have thought to compile the recorded sayings of the various venerable masters of the Ming dynasty.
I have compiled biographies and stele inscriptions into a single volume to await a future author.

Yet, upon extensively searching through literary collections and historical records, I find that all biographies of immortals and Buddhist monks have been excised by vulgar scholars. With only a few meager accounts remaining, I am deeply ashamed of my own ignorance and paucity of learning.
Furthermore, being of advanced age and failing faculties, I am unable to travel far to seek them out.
I venture to inscribe this to inform the venerable elders of the monasteries and lay practitioners in the great cities and capitals:

if there exist records of the sayings, biographies, funerary inscriptions, or gazetteers of temples concerning Master Ming of our lineage, other than those currently circulating at Lêng-yen Monastery in Chia-hsing, please do not withhold them.

I pray that you will graciously instruct me on all fragments and scattered passages from the collected drafts of your commentaries—whether a single character or a single phrase—that may benefit the transmission of the Lamp.
This shall allow me to compile them for publication, serving as an aid for the future continuation of the Lamp.
By thus elucidating the Dharma-treasure and perpetuating the Buddha’s wisdom-life, the merit thereof is truly immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.
In the fifth month of summer in the Renwu year of the Chongzhen era, the Layman of Lize, Shi Pei of Huating, sets forth the preface and rules for this compilation.
Although this work has been compiled and assembled into a book, it is still titled *Cungao* (Drafts); this is because the hand-touched traces of my late teacher have not yet [been fully processed].
I venture to transmit this hastily. I await those who will come in the future with the resolve to continue the transmission of the Lamp.

Although the *Ji-zong* (Record of the Ji Lineage) already contains the eighteenth generation of Dajian [Huangbo] at the end of its final fascicle, I have recorded it here again because what was included in the *Huiyuan* (Compendium of Essentials) was incomplete.
The ancestral lineage of the Caodong school all traces back to Master Yuan; thus, [Zongmi] continued the *Lue* by treating Yuan as the son of Yunmen.
If this were not the case, Sun Liang would incur the fault of falsely usurping his ancestors' heritage.
This book is intended exclusively for the circulation of the essential eye of our school. Dharma discourses that have not yet found the appropriate opportunity for transmission shall not be included.
However, regarding those whose lineage and origins are known in broad outline, these shall be recorded here to serve as a basis for future research.
According to Dàchuān’s *Huìyuán*, Dàhuì is listed before Hǔqiū; according to Cuìfēng’s *Xùchúndēng*, Hǔqiū is listed before Dàhuì.
Yuǎnhuì’s *Huìyuán-xùlüè* places the Dòngzōng (Cave School) at the beginning of the first volume.
Critics have remarked that each [compiler] honors their own ancestral lineage, fearing this may not reflect the ultimate intent of the original authors. When measured against the facts...
Each meaning is appropriate to its context. For the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) is not the book of a single school;

how could one harbor views that elevate one’s own tradition while disparaging others? Now, Linji and Caodong generally follow their traditional precedents, collectively designating the generations of Dajian [Huineng] as the "Xth" or "Yth" generation.

This is done so that they may be read conveniently according to the specific requirements of these two schools, rather than being interspersed with the chronological order found in the *Huiyuan*. Furthermore—
This is not because there is anything external to them. I have not yet fully detailed their dharma lineages, so they are appended here at the end.
The Ji (Linji) school begins with the eighteenth generation from Dajian (Mazu) and ends with the thirty-fourth generation.
The Dong (Caodong) school begins with the sixteenth generation from Dajian and ends with the thirty-sixth generation. This constitutes the twelfth fascicle.
Volume Six of the Collected Works. Respectfully composed by Xu Yuhua.
